title: Why Did the Leader Cross the Road?
author: Dan Korus
summary: A leadership and emotional-intelligence consultant opens with a personal anecdote -- a CEO who weaponized the self-help book The Four Agreements against him, using 'don't take anything personally' to reframe the CEO's own threatening email as the author's problem rather than the CEO's -- to introduce the essay's reworking of the Good Samaritan parable: leaders 'cross the road' not from ignorance of what's needed, but because doing the emotional work of leadership is inconvenient. The bulk of the piece assembles peer-reviewed research linking leader emotional intelligence to four organizational outcomes: revenue growth (a study of 229 Canadian entrepreneurs found positive emotional climate predicted revenue growth 18 months later), reduced turnover, earlier risk detection (safety-climate improvements in ICUs correlated with 33% lower odds of reported medication or equipment errors), and greater innovation (psychological safety, driven by inclusive leadership, predicted employees' involvement in creative work). Its sharpest observation is a pattern the author hears repeatedly when pitching EQ workshops: leaders want the revenue, retention, risk-reduction, and innovation benefits that flow from a high-EQ workplace, while resisting the personal emotional-regulation work required to actually build one. The essay closes by reframing the parable's central failure: the priest and Levite in the original story didn't cross the road out of ignorance, but because stopping would have cost them time and discomfort -- exactly the excuse the essay accuses leaders of making about their own emotional development.
points: The opening anecdote demonstrates a specific misuse pattern: a self-help principle about personal accountability ('don't take anything personally') gets redirected by the more powerful party to apply only to the person receiving harm, not the person causing it -- a template readers can recognize in their own workplaces.

The safety-climate research is the essay's most concrete causal chain: among 795 patients across 57 ICUs, a one-standard-deviation improvement in safety climate was associated with 33% lower odds of a reported medication or equipment error, directly tying leader-driven psychological safety to a measurable harm-reduction outcome.

The essay's most pointed diagnostic is the pattern it names explicitly: leaders resist EQ development by asking 'what's the ROI?' while simultaneously wanting the exact revenue, retention, safety, and innovation outcomes the cited research shows only flow from doing that development work.

The reworked Good Samaritan moral -- the priest and Levite crossed the road not from ignorance but because stopping cost them time, discomfort, and obligation -- reframes leadership avoidance of emotional-intelligence work as a choice, not a knowledge gap, which is the essay's central accusation against reluctant leaders.
quotes: Don't take anything personally" became a standard for the person receiving the threat, not the person making it. He had turned a lesson about personal accountability into a way to escape his own.
When leaders refuse to work on their emotional intelligence, they cross the road, leaving the community to deal with the wounds.
In 253 electronics stores employing 1,611 people, manager emotional intelligence predicted store cohesion, which predicted sales directed behavior, which predicted store performance.
Across 57 ICUs and 795 patients, a one standard deviation improvement in safety climate was associated with 33% lower odds of a reported medication or equipment error.

Yet leaders want the revenue created by cohesion, the retention created by care, the risk reduction created by candor, and the innovation created by psychological safety. These benefits begin at the top. Culture travels downhill with brutal efficiency.
They crossed because stopping would have cost them time, discomfort, proximity and obligation. The question is whether we're willing to stop crossing the road.
